lead: Non-functional testing measures qualities, not features. Performance testing asks how fast the system answers under expected load. Stress testing asks what happens beyond capacity and whether the system recovers. Configuration testing asks whether one product works across hardware, operating systems, browsers and networks. Usability testing asks whether real users can finish their tasks, including users who need a keyboard, a screen reader, large text or high contrast. A ticket site that is correct but takes 8 seconds on a booking day fails its users. These tests turn qualities into numbers you can check.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for expected versus actual behaviour, and Chapter 4.6 for system testing; Unit 3, User interface design for usability goals.

blocks.text: Performance testing is the umbrella term for measuring speed and capacity under a stated workload. Response time is the time from sending a request to receiving the full reply, in seconds. Throughput is the number of completed requests divided by the observation time, in requests per second. Resource use covers CPU percentage, memory in MB and network in Mbps. Within it, load testing runs the system at the anticipated load, including the expected peak such as 10,000 virtual users on a ticket site; stress testing (Section 2) goes beyond that peak.

blocks.where: completed requests is the count finished in the window; observation time is the window length in seconds; throughput is in requests per second.

blocks.text: A virtual user is a software thread that sends requests like a person, with think time — the seconds a person spends reading before the next click. Report the 95th percentile response time: 95% of requests were faster than this value. The average hides the slow users who complain.

items: Define the target: 95% of searches under 3 s at 10,000 virtual users.
Build a workload mix: 70% search, 20% seat view, 10% payment.
Ramp up virtual users and hold the peak for 10 minutes.
Record response time, throughput, errors, CPU and memory.
Compare with the target and with the previous release.

blocks.text: Stress testing pushes beyond the expected peak until the system breaks or degrades. It answers three questions: where is the breaking point, does the system fail safely, and does it recover? For the ticket site, a stress run uses 20,000 virtual users. Response time is 5.6 s and some requests fail. A safe system queues work or shows a wait page; it does not lose a payment.

Recovery is part of the test. Drop the load back to 5,000 users and check that response time returns to 1.4 s and no data is corrupted. A soak test holds a moderate load for hours to find memory leaks and disk filling. Stress is not the same as performance: performance checks the target, stress checks the limit and the way back.

Configuration testing runs the same tests on a matrix of supported environments: hardware (phone, tablet, desktop), operating system versions, browser versions, screen sizes and network speeds such as 4G and throttled 3G. A full matrix is too large, so choose by risk or use pairwise combinations. Compatibility testing checks versions and devices, including older Android versions still in use.

Internationalisation testing checks language, currency, date and number formats. The same number is grouped ₹1,23,456.78 in India (lakh grouping: 1,23,456) and 123,456.78 in the US (thousand grouping). The currency symbol is also part of the locale; the actual amount depends on the exchange rate. A date 03/04/2025 means 3 April in India and 4 March in the US. German text may be 30% longer than English and break a button. Test the locale, not just the translation.

Usability testing watches real users, not developers, attempt representative tasks. A moderator gives a task: “Book a train ticket from Chennai to Bengaluru for tomorrow.” Record completion rate, time on task, errors and satisfaction. In the example, 8 of 10 users complete a booking in 2 minutes; the two failures show where the form confuses people. Think-aloud asks users to speak their thoughts as they work.

Accessibility testing checks that people with disabilities can use the product. Keyboard only: every action is reachable without a mouse. Screen reader: images have text alternatives and form fields have labels. Contrast: normal text is at least 4.5:1 against its background. Text size: the layout survives 200% zoom. Captions make video usable without sound. Accessibility is usability testing with a specific user group and specific checks.

spec.aria: A line chart of 95th-percentile response time against virtual users, through 1.4 s at 5,000, 2.8 at 10,000, 4.2 at 15,000 and 5.6 at 20,000. A dashed line at 3 seconds is crossed at about 10,714 users.

examples.question: A ticket booking site is load-tested with 10,000 virtual users for 10 minutes. The target is 95% of searches under 3 s. Measured 95th-percentile response times: 1.4 s at 5,000 users, 2.8 s at 10,000 users, 4.2 s at 15,000 users, 5.6 s at 20,000 users. At peak the site completes 10,000 searches in 50 s. (a) Compute throughput in searches per second. (b) Estimate the highest number of virtual users that keeps response time at or under 3 s by linear interpolation between the two nearest points. (c) State one stress test, one configuration test and one usability test with numbers.
steps: (a) Throughput = completed requests ÷ observation time = 10,000 searches ÷ 50 s = 200 searches per second.
(b) The target 3.0 s lies between 10,000 users (2.8 s) and 15,000 users (4.2 s). Slope = (4.2 − 2.8) s ÷ (15,000 − 10,000) users = 1.4 ÷ 5,000 = 0.00028 s per user.
Extra time allowed = 3.0 − 2.8 = 0.2 s. Extra users = 0.2 ÷ 0.00028 = 714.29 users.

(c) Stress: run 20,000 users; response is 5.6 s and errors appear; drop to 5,000 users and check response returns to 1.4 s. Configuration: Chrome and Firefox on Windows 11 desktop, and two Android versions on a phone; complete a booking on each. Usability: 10 real users attempt a booking; 8 complete within 2 minutes.
examples.answer: Throughput is 200 searches per second; the 3 s target is met up to about 10,714 virtual users; a stress run at 20,000 users gives 5.6 s and must recover; configuration and usability runs as listed.
examples.check:
throughput = 10000 / 50
print(throughput)
x1, y1 = 10000, 2.8
x2, y2 = 15000, 4.2
slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
limit = x1 + (3.0 - y1) / slope
print(round(limit, 2))

traps: Stress testing is not the same as load testing: stress goes beyond the expected peak and checks recovery.
A response-time average hides slow users; use the 95th percentile for the target.
Throughput is requests per second, not seconds per request; seconds per request is response time.
Testing on one developer phone is not configuration testing; configuration testing uses a matrix of supported environments.
A usability test with developers or with one colleague is not a usability test; use representative real users.

quiz.q: Define throughput and give its unit.
quiz.a: Throughput is the number of completed requests divided by the observation time. Its unit is requests per second.

quiz.q: Why is stress testing done after load testing?
quiz.a: Load testing confirms the system meets its target at the expected peak. Stress testing then pushes beyond that peak to find the breaking point, check safe failure, and check recovery.

quiz.q: A service completes 12,000 requests in 60 s. Compute throughput.
Response time is 2.0 s at 4,000 users and 3.2 s at 8,000 users. Estimate by linear interpolation the users at which response time reaches 3.0 s.
A team tests a web app only on one laptop with Chrome and calls it configuration testing. What is wrong, and what should they do?
quiz.a: One laptop with one browser is a single configuration. They should test a risk-based matrix of supported operating systems, browsers, screen sizes and network speeds, including older versions still in use.

quiz.q: In a usability test, 9 of 10 users complete the task, but the average time is 4 minutes against a 2-minute target. Is the task usable? Explain.
quiz.a: Completion is high, but the time target is missed by 2 minutes. The task is learnable but too slow; examine the steps that take longest and retest. Report both completion rate and time, not one number alone.

quiz.q: Give two accessibility checks and what each catches.
quiz.a: Keyboard-only navigation catches actions reachable only by mouse. Screen-reader labels catch unlabelled form fields and images without text alternatives.

quiz.q: A site shows ₹1,23,456.78 in India and $123,456.78 in the US. Which type of testing checks this?
quiz.a: Internationalisation (i18n) testing checks currency, number and date formats for each locale. This chapter covers it in the same section as configuration testing, but it is a separate type of test.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, load tests run in delivery pipelines with scripted virtual users and results feed service-level objectives. Observability links a slow response to a database query or a network hop. Accessibility is becoming a legal requirement for public digital services. Search for “load testing percentile latency”, “pairwise testing”, “WCAG quick reference” and “internationalisation testing checklist”.
